title: 1958–1967: The Golden Years
tagline: Steady industrial expansion · Rise of high-end manufacturing · Two dollar crises · Vietnam escalation and the return of inflation

sections.heading: Era Tone
body: 1958–1968 was the 'golden age' of the US economy. Industrial production grew at an average monthly year-over-year rate of 5.2% — slightly higher than the 5.0% of 1948–1957, but with far less volatility. The decade opened in the trough of the first postwar globally synchronized recession, was punctuated by two dollar crises, the Cuban Missile Crisis, the Kennedy assassination, and the escalation of the Vietnam War, and ended with the de facto collapse of Bretton Woods (the two-tier gold system).

The most striking economic shift: macro and micro fully aligned for the first time. Using 1957 as a base, by 1968 nominal GDP was up 98.4%, pre-tax corporate profits up 91.2%, and after-tax profits up 100.4%. The previous decade's gap of 'macro boom plus lagging corporate earnings' had closed.

items.body: Q1 1958 GDP was −2.9% year-over-year and unemployment hit 7.4% in April. Recovery began mid-year, and 1959 GDP rose 6.9%. The Fed cut rates to 1.75% in early 1958, turned to tightening mid-year, and hiked three times by 50bp each in 1959; the discount rate ended at 4.0%.

items.strong: 1960–1962: The Triffin Dilemma and the First Dollar Crisis
items.body: Cumulative US balance-of-payments deficits exceeded $11 billion in 1958–1960, and gold reserves fell from $22.77 billion to $17.95 billion. October 1960 brought the first postwar wave of dollar dumping for gold. From 1961 the Fed adopted 'Operation Twist': lending rather than cutting, pressing long-end yields down while keeping the short end steady. Q1 1962 GDP bottomed at −0.7%, and the full year recovered to above 6%.

GDP growth rose from 4.4% in 1963 to 6.6% in 1966, supported mainly by consumer spending. CPI held at a low 1.3% until the second half of 1965, when Vietnam-related spending began pushing it higher. In July 1963 the Fed hiked for the first time on its own initiative (3.0% to 3.5%), and the Interest Equalization Tax was enacted that year to curb capital outflows. The Voluntary Foreign Credit Restraint program (VFCR) launched in 1965.

items.strong: 1967–1968: The Second Dollar Crisis and the Two-Tier Gold System
items.body: GDP growth slowed to 2.7% in 1967 while inflation kept climbing: CPI rose to 3.1% and accelerated to 4.2% in 1968 (core CPI at 4.6%, a multi-decade high). March 1968 brought the second dollar crisis: gold reserves bled out by more than $1.4 billion in half a month. On March 17 the US and seven Western European countries agreed on the two-tier gold system — official price at $35/oz, market price floating — and the gold pool was dissolved.

sections.heading: Economic Structure: From Traditional to High-End Manufacturing
body: The three pillar industries remained unchanged: manufacturing (25% of GDP), wholesale and retail trade (14%), and finance and real estate (14%). But internal differentiation intensified: the tertiary sector (education and health 9.9%, business services 8.0%, information 7.5%, finance and real estate 7.1%) led nominal value-added growth, while the primary sector (agriculture, forestry, fishing 2.3%) and traditional secondary sectors (mining 1.5%) kept shrinking.

Inside manufacturing, the divide between 'high-end' and 'traditional' was the most visible: computers and electronics led at 8.1%, plastics and rubber at 7.6%, electrical equipment 7.0%, and autos and parts 6.9%. Petroleum and coal at 2.1%, primary metals at 3.0%, and nonmetallic minerals at 4.2% were the laggards. This was the decade in which US manufacturing pivoted from the 'steel-and-auto era' to 'high-tech plus durable consumer goods'.

Overseas profits' share slipped from 10.2% in 1957 to 9.3% in 1968, but absolute levels kept rising sharply. Services' share of profits more than doubled from 1.4% to 3.7%, becoming structurally meaningful. Mining's share of profits slid from 3.2% to 1.0% — the largest drop outside manufacturing.

sections.heading: Taxes: Successive Cuts to Spur Capital
body: The Kennedy–Johnson administrations' supply-side reforms came in three steps. The Revenue Act of 1962 introduced the 7% investment tax credit (effective tax rate from 41% to 39%); the Revenue Act of 1964 cut the top corporate rate from 52% to 48% (effective rate to 37%); and the Revenue and Expenditure Control Act of 1968, responding to Vietnam-era inflation, clawed back some of those cuts with a temporary 10% corporate surtax (effective rate back to 38%).
This was the first postwar policy experiment built around 'tax cuts to spur private investment.' It explains why corporate after-tax profits consistently outpaced pre-tax profits from 1962 to 1968.

items.body: The first postwar wave of dollar dumping for gold; the Triffin Dilemma was vindicated, and confidence in the dollar wavered.
items.title: First Dollar Crisis

items.body: On August 13, East Germany began building the Berlin Wall, freezing the Cold War in physical form.
items.title: Berlin Wall Built

items.body: October 14–28: a 13-day US-Soviet standoff — the closest humanity has come to nuclear war.
items.title: Cuban Missile Crisis

items.body: President Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas at 12:30 pm on November 22. Lyndon Johnson succeeded him.
items.title: Kennedy Assassination

items.body: Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964, ending de jure segregation, and launched the 'War on Poverty' social-program expansion.
items.title: Civil Rights Act and War on Poverty

items.body: The US committed large-scale ground forces in Vietnam. French President de Gaulle continued converting dollars to gold and shipping it home, intensifying the dollar crisis.
items.title: Vietnam Escalation and France Takes Its Gold

items.body: On November 18, sterling was devalued 14.3%; turmoil in the European monetary system spread to the dollar.
items.title: Sterling Crisis

items.body: The March 17 Washington Agreement left the official $35/oz dollar-gold parity in name only; Bretton Woods began unraveling.
items.title: Two-Tier Gold System
